title: Place Value in Grade 2: Hundreds, Tens and Ones Made Simple + Free Quiz
meta_title: Place Value Grade 2: Hundreds, Tens & Ones Guide
meta_desc: Teach place value in Grade 2 the right way: hundreds, tens and ones, expanded form and face value, with a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: The moment a child sees that the 2 in 245 means two hundred, not just two, arithmetic stops being guesswork. Here is how to teach hundreds, tens and ones in Grade 2, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 245 on a slate and ask a Grade 2 child what the 2 means. Most will say ‘two’. The whole of Grade 2 maths rests on them eventually answering ‘two hundred’ — and understanding place value in Grade 2, the idea that hundreds, tens and ones each sit in their own column, is the single most important thing a seven-year-old learns all year. Get this right and column addition, subtraction with borrowing, even three-digit comparison all fall into place later. Get it wrong and every one of those topics becomes a struggle.

I have taught this to plenty of Tier-2 city classrooms where children can happily rattle off numbers to 100 but freeze at 3-digit numbers. The fix is almost never more counting. It is making the columns concrete first, then abstract. Here is the order that works.

Why place value is the idea that unlocks Grade 2

Our number system is positional. The same digit means a different amount depending on where it sits. In 245 the 2 is worth 200, the 4 is worth 40, and the 5 is worth 5. Move the digits — 452 — and now the 2 is worth only 2. Nothing else in Grade 2 arithmetic makes sense until this lands.

The counter-intuitive bit worth telling parents: a child who can count to 500 has not necessarily understood place value at all. Counting is a chant. Place value is structure. They are different skills, and Grade 2 is where the second one has to be built deliberately.

Start with bundles, not symbols

Before any child writes hundreds, tens and ones in a chart, they should build them. NCERT and every good Grade 2 teacher I know uses the same tool: base-ten blocks, or, if you have none, bundles of ten sticks (matchsticks, ice-cream sticks) tied with a rubber band.

  • A single loose stick is a one.
  • Ten sticks tied together is a ten.
  • Ten bundles of ten — a hundred sticks — is a hundred.

Now 245 is not an abstract squiggle. It is 2 big hundred-bundles, 4 ten-bundles, and 5 loose sticks on the desk. Ask the child to make 132, then 300, then 208 (the zero trips them up beautifully — ‘no tens’ is a real thing to see). Ten minutes of building beats an hour of worksheets at this stage.

The place-value chart: hundreds, tens and ones

Once bundles are secure, move to the chart. Draw three columns and drop the digits in. This is the bridge from the desk to the page.

NumberHundreds (H)Tens (T)Ones (O)Read as
245245200 + 40 + 5
307307300 + 0 + 7
560560500 + 60 + 0
108108100 + 0 + 8

Notice how the chart forces the child to confront the zero. In 307 there are no tens, so a 0 must hold the tens column open. Without that 0 the 3 and the 7 would slide together into 37 — a completely different number. That single insight prevents a whole class of Grade 2 errors.

Expanded form: 245 = 200 + 40 + 5

Expanded form is just the place-value chart written as a sum. It is the clearest proof that a child has understood the columns, and it is worth drilling until it is automatic.

Say each digit as its true value: 245 is two hundred, forty, five, so 245 = 200 + 40 + 5. Going backwards is just as important — give the child 500 + 30 + 6 and ask for the standard number (536). When both directions come easily, the concept is solid. Watch for the trap in numbers like 405: children love to write 400 + 50 + 5 instead of 400 + 0 + 5. That mistake tells you the tens column has not clicked yet.

Face value versus place value

This is the distinction Grade 2 exams love to ask about, and it confuses children because the two words sound similar.

  • Face value is simply the digit itself — what it looks like. In 245, the face value of the 4 is just 4.
  • Place value is what the digit is worth because of its column. In 245, the place value of the 4 is 40, because it sits in the tens place.

A neat way to lock it in: for any digit except those in the ones column, the face value and place value are different. The face value of 2 in 245 is 2; its place value is 200. Only the ones digit has a face value equal to its place value. Ask a child ‘what is the face value of the 5 in 356, and what is its place value?’ — both are 5, because it is in the ones place. That is not a trick; it is the definition working exactly as it should.

A simple weekly routine that works

Ten minutes a day, five days a week, beats a marathon session. A pattern that has served parents well:

  • Two days building numbers with bundles and reading them aloud.
  • One day filling a hundreds-tens-ones chart from spoken numbers.
  • One day on expanded form, both directions.
  • One day mixing face value and place value questions on paper so the child has to decide which is being asked.

One honest caveat: do not rush to three digits if two-digit place value is shaky. A child who is fuzzy on tens and ones will only get more lost when hundreds arrive. Spend the extra week — it pays back all year.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly what we have talked about — hundreds, tens and ones, expanded form, and the face-value-versus-place-value difference. Let your child attempt it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded place-value questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Place Value Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on hundreds, tens and ones, expanded form and face value. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 2 place value up to 3-digit numbers

questions.q: In the number 245, what is the place value of the digit 2?
questions.explanation: The 2 sits in the hundreds column, so its place value is 200.

questions.q: Which number is 300 + 40 + 6 in standard form?
How many tens are in the number 570?
questions.explanation: The digit in the tens column of 570 is 7, so there are 7 tens.

questions.q: What is the expanded form of 208?
questions.explanation: There are no tens, so a 0 holds the tens place: 208 = 200 + 0 + 8.

questions.q: In 356, what is the face value of the digit 3?
questions.explanation: Face value is just the digit itself, so the face value of 3 is 3.

questions.q: Which number has 4 hundreds, 0 tens and 7 ones?
questions.explanation: 4 hundreds and 7 ones with no tens is written 407, using 0 to hold the tens place.

questions.q: What is the place value of 5 in the number 356?
questions.explanation: The 5 is in the tens column, so its place value is 50.

questions.q: Which number is the same as 500 + 60?
questions.explanation: 5 hundreds and 6 tens with no ones make 560.

faq.q: What place value topics should a Grade 2 child know?
faq.a: By the end of Grade 2 a child should read and write 3-digit numbers, name the hundreds, tens and ones in any number, write expanded form such as 245 = 200 + 40 + 5, and tell face value apart from place value.

faq.q: What is the difference between face value and place value?
faq.a: Face value is the digit itself — the face value of 4 in 245 is just 4. Place value is what the digit is worth in its column — the place value of that same 4 is 40, because it sits in the tens place.

faq.q: How do I teach place value without any special materials?
faq.a: Bundle ten matchsticks or ice-cream sticks with a rubber band to make a ten, and ten of those bundles to make a hundred. Loose sticks are ones. Building numbers by hand makes the columns concrete before you move to a chart.

faq.q: Why does my child write 405 as 400 + 50 + 5?
faq.a: It means the tens column has not clicked yet. The correct expanded form is 400 + 0 + 5. Go back to bundles and show that 405 has no ten-bundles at all, so the tens place must hold a 0.
